messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Aleksandr Petrov

Aleksandr Petrov was twenty-one when he arrived at the intake appointment—a tall, lean man with dark hair and the careful posture of someone used to taking up as little space as possible. He had been in the United States for three years, having fled Syria with his mother and younger sister when he was eighteen. His English was fluent but precise, each word chosen as though he were still translating in his head. He worked as a public defender's paralegal, a position he had secured through a legal aid internship after his first year of college. On paper, his life looked like a recovery story: he had rebuilt, moved forward, found stability. But the way he sat in the chair—legs angled toward the door, hands folded tightly in his lap—suggested something very different.

The traumatic event itself had occurred over days rather than hours. In the spring of 2019, Aleksandr's neighborhood in Aleppo had come under sustained bombardment. He and his family had sheltered in their apartment building's basement with thirty other people, listening to the percussion of explosions that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The sounds were not discrete—they were a continuous, unpredictable assault. What haunted him most was not the noise itself but the silences between explosions. In those moments of quiet, Aleksandr had become certain that the next strike would be the one that collapsed the building. He had crouched in the dark, his body pressed against the concrete wall, waiting for death. On the fourth day, a shell struck nearby, killing two neighbors. His family escaped that night. But Aleksandr's nervous system had learned something in that basement: silence was not safety. Silence was the moment before catastrophe.

Three years later, ordinary sounds still shattered him. A car backfiring on the street outside the courthouse where he worked sent him into a crouch. The sound of a door slamming in the office made his heart accelerate for minutes afterward. His colleagues had begun to notice. One morning, when a paralegal dropped a stack of case files, Aleksandr had jumped so violently that he knocked over his coffee. He had made an excuse about being tired, but the shame had burned through him. What frightened him most was not the startle itself but what it meant: that he was not recovering, that his mind was broken in some fundamental way, that one day at work he would react so badly that everyone would see he did not belong in a professional setting.

This fear had led him to develop an elaborate internal monitoring system. He had come to believe that if he could catch his own thoughts before they spiraled, if he could notice when he was being irrational, then perhaps he could prevent himself from having a complete breakdown. Throughout the workday, he was constantly scanning his own mind for signs of unreasonableness. When his girlfriend, Zara, had asked him what he was thinking about during dinner one evening, he had frozen. He could not tell her that he had been monitoring whether the restaurant's quiet moment—the lull between the lunch and dinner rush—meant something was about to go wrong. He could not explain that he was watching himself watch for danger, and that this recursive vigilance was exhausting. Instead, he had said nothing. She had asked again, more gently, and he had deflected with a question about her work. Over the following weeks, Zara had tried multiple times to talk with him about the trauma, about what he had experienced. Each time, Aleksandr had found a way to leave the room—a phone call to make, a document to review, a sudden need to shower. Talking about the event felt like it would confirm that he was still unsafe, that the danger had not actually passed.

His memories arrived as fragmented sensations. Sometimes it was purely visual—the concrete wall of the basement, the darkness, the small window high up that showed only gray sky. Other times, his body would suddenly remember before his mind caught up. He would find himself crouched, his shoulders hunched, his back against something solid, with no conscious awareness of why. The most distressing memories were the ones without images at all—moments when he would be sitting at his desk reviewing case files and would be flooded with the exact emotional state of those four days: the absolute conviction that danger was imminent, the suffocating dread, the sense that the world was fundamentally hostile and that only constant vigilance could keep him alive.

This belief had become the lens through which he saw everything. The world was dangerous. It always had been, and it always would be. People in his office who seemed relaxed, who did not check their surroundings constantly, struck him as naive or lucky. He had to be on guard all the time. He had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. This was not paranoia—this was truth, earned through experience. When his supervisor had suggested he take on a new case involving a client with a history of violence, Aleksandr had felt his stomach drop. He had accepted anyway, but for two weeks before the first meeting, he had researched the client's arrest history obsessively, had mapped out exits in the interview room, had positioned himself so that he was never between the client and the door.

It was Zara who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed that he was disappearing into himself, that their conversations had become surface-level, that he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly. She had also noticed that he was drinking more—not heavily, but with a kind of grim consistency, a way of quieting the constant internal noise. She had told him, with a directness he appreciated, that she could not watch him suffer alone anymore. The word *suffer* had struck him. He had not thought of himself as suffering. He had thought of himself as managing, as surviving, as doing what was necessary. But when she said it, he recognized it as true. He was suffering. And for the first time since arriving in America, he allowed himself to ask for help.
